junior.title: Never hides an error
good_looks_like: Every caught error is handled, logged with context, or thrown again. Nothing is caught and silently dropped.
explain_angles: What happens to the user when this error is caught here?
Who finds out that this failed, and how?

drills.prompt: A teammate wraps a database save in try/catch with an empty catch block 'so the request never crashes'. What goes wrong, and what would you do instead?

key_points.text: The failure becomes invisible: data is lost and nobody knows
The caller wrongly believes the save worked
Either handle it on purpose, or log with context and let it fail to the caller

red_flags.text: Says an empty catch is fine as long as nothing crashes

drills.prompt: When is it right to catch an error and NOT throw it again? Give an example and say what you must still do.

key_points.text: When there is a real fallback or the failure does not matter to the result
A concrete example such as an optional cache or a best-effort metric
Still log or count it so the failure is visible

red_flags.text: Says it is fine to catch any error and move on

study: error handling basics in your language

express.note: Pass errors to next(err) and keep one error-handling middleware; never end a request from an empty catch.

nestjs.note: Throw an HttpException or a custom one and let an exception filter shape the reply; do not swallow it in the service.

spring.note: Let exceptions reach a @ControllerAdvice handler; do not catch and ignore them in the service.

junior.title: Checks the result of calls that can fail
good_looks_like: Checks for missing rows, null results and failed status codes before using the result.
explain_angles: What happens here if the call returns nothing?
Why check it here and not later?

drills.prompt: Your endpoint loads an order by id and then reads order.customer.email. What can go wrong, and how do you handle each case?

key_points.text: The order may not exist: return a clear 404
The customer or email may be missing: decide what the caller gets
Check before use instead of letting a null error become a 500

red_flags.text: Lets a null reference error reach the user as a 500

drills.prompt: An outside API returns HTTP 200 with a body like { ok: false, error: 'quota' }. How should your code treat it?

key_points.text: A 200 status does not mean success; read the body's own status
Turn it into a real error in your code
Decide whether it is worth retrying or should be shown to the caller

express.note: Return 404 for a missing resource with a short JSON body; check results before using them.

nestjs.note: Throw NotFoundException when a lookup finds nothing.

spring.note: Use Optional from repositories and orElseThrow a not-found exception.

mid.title: Validates input at the edge
good_looks_like: Checks request input once, where it enters the system, and rejects bad input with a clear 400 that says what is wrong.
explain_angles: Why validate here and not deeper in the code?
What does the caller see for bad input?

drills.prompt: A create-user endpoint takes name, email and age. Where and how do you validate them, and what does a client get back for bad input?

key_points.text: Validate at the entry point with a schema
Return 400 with which fields are wrong and why
Inner code can then trust its input instead of checking again everywhere

red_flags.text: Relies on the frontend to validate

drills.prompt: Why is checking input only in the browser not enough? Give one attack or bug it lets through.

key_points.text: Anyone can call the API directly and skip the browser
A concrete example: a negative quantity, a huge string, a wrong type
The server is the only place the rule is enforced

express.note: Validate req.body with a schema library in a middleware and reply 400 with field errors.

nestjs.note: Use DTOs with class-validator and the global ValidationPipe.

spring.note: Use @Valid on request bodies with Bean Validation annotations.

mid.title: Handles the failure of an outside call on purpose
good_looks_like: Sets a time limit on every call to another service.
Retries only when it is safe, with backoff, and gives the caller a clear error when it still fails.
explain_angles: Why this time limit, and what happens when it runs out?
Is it safe to retry this call? Why?
What does the caller see when the outside service is down?

drills.prompt: Your service calls a payment provider that sometimes takes 30 seconds to answer. How do you design the call? What can go wrong with retries?

key_points.text: Set a time limit shorter than your own caller's
Retry only with an idempotency key, or not at all, so a charge is never made twice
Backoff with jitter and a small retry cap
A clear error or 'pending' state for the caller when it still fails

red_flags.text: Retries a payment with no idempotency key

drills.prompt: A downstream service is down for 10 minutes. Your service retries every failed call 5 times right away. What happens, and what would you change?

key_points.text: Retries multiply the load and slow down your own service
Use backoff with jitter and a retry cap
Fail fast or use a circuit breaker while it is down

express.note: Pass AbortSignal.timeout(ms) to fetch; retry only idempotent calls, with backoff.

nestjs.note: Set a timeout on HttpModule and use rxjs timeout and retry with a delay function.

spring.note: Set connect and read timeouts on the client; use Resilience4j for retry and circuit breaker.

mid.title: Errors carry useful context without leaking data
good_looks_like: A new error keeps its cause and says what was being done.
The client gets a safe message; stack traces and internal details stay in the logs.
explain_angles: What will the person debugging this see in the logs?
What does the client see, and why not more?

drills.prompt: A user reports 'it failed' and your log says only 'Error: undefined'. How should errors be written so this never happens again, and what should the user see?

key_points.text: Wrap errors with what was being done and keep the original cause
Log with an id that links the request and the error
The user gets a safe message plus the id, never the stack trace

red_flags.text: Sends the stack trace to the client

drills.prompt: Why is res.status(500).json(err) a problem? What would you send instead?

key_points.text: It can leak internals: stack, SQL, file paths, secrets
Send a stable error shape with a safe message and a code
Keep full details in the server logs

red_flags.text: Says the raw error helps the client debug

express.note: Throw new Error(msg, { cause }) and map errors to safe JSON in one error middleware.

nestjs.note: Use an exception filter to return a safe shape and log the full error.

spring.note: Return ProblemDetail from @ExceptionHandler and keep the cause in the log.

senior.title: Designs for partial failure
good_looks_like: When one step of a multi-step change fails, the system ends in a known state: retried safely, compensated, or clearly marked for follow-up.
explain_angles: What state is the data in if the second step fails?
How does this recover without a person?

drills.prompt: An order flow charges the card, then reserves stock, then sends an email. Stock reservation fails after the charge. How do you design this?

key_points.text: Name the bad state: money taken, no stock
Compensate (refund) or retry the step, with idempotent steps
Record progress so a crash mid-flow can resume (outbox, saga, or state machine)
Side effects like email only after the important steps succeed

red_flags.text: Assumes all steps succeed or fail together without a transaction that covers them

drills.prompt: You must save a row and publish an event about it. What can go wrong, and how do you make sure both happen?

key_points.text: The save can succeed and the publish fail, or the other way round
Use a transactional outbox or similar
Consumers must handle duplicates

red_flags.text: Publishes before the save commits and calls it done

express.note: Keep each step idempotent and record progress in the database before side effects.

nestjs.note: Use a queue (for example BullMQ) for steps after the main transaction, with retries.

spring.note: Use @TransactionalEventListener or an outbox table to publish after commit.

senior.title: Makes failures observable
good_looks_like: Failures show up as structured logs, metrics and alerts that tell someone what broke, before users report it.
explain_angles: How would you know this is failing in production?
Who gets alerted, and on what?

drills.prompt: Your checkout fails for 2% of users and nobody noticed for a week. What would you add so this is caught in minutes?

key_points.text: An error-rate metric on the checkout path
An alert on that rate with a sensible threshold
Structured logs with a request id to find the cause

red_flags.text: Relies on users or support tickets to notice

drills.prompt: What makes a log line useful during an incident? Compare a good and a bad one.

key_points.text: Structured fields, not free text
Request or trace id, and what was being done
No secrets or personal data

red_flags.text: Logs full request bodies with personal data

express.note: Use a structured logger (for example pino) with a request id per request.

nestjs.note: Replace the default logger with a structured one and add an interceptor for request ids.

spring.note: Use Actuator and Micrometer for metrics, and MDC for request ids in logs.

staff.title: Sets the error-handling standard for a system
good_looks_like: Defines one error contract, retry and timeout rules, and error budgets that every team follows, and makes the easy path the right one.
explain_angles: Why should every service follow this rule?
How do you make the right way the easy way?

drills.prompt: Ten services each handle errors their own way, and incidents are hard to trace. What standard would you set, and how would you roll it out?

key_points.text: One error shape and code list across services
Shared defaults for time limits, retries and tracing, in a library or template
Roll out step by step with checks in CI or review
Measure success with error budgets or incident data

red_flags.text: Only writes a document and expects people to follow it

drills.prompt: How would you choose time limits and retry budgets across a chain of four services calling each other?

key_points.text: Time limits shrink down the chain so the caller's budget is respected
Retry at one layer only to avoid retry storms
Pass the deadline along with the request

express.note: Ship a shared middleware package for errors, timeouts and request ids.

nestjs.note: Ship a shared module with a global filter, interceptor and HTTP client defaults.

spring.note: Ship a starter with ProblemDetail handling, Resilience4j defaults and tracing.
